title: The Black Death (1348)
hookLine: Jews are blamed for the plague and whole communities murdered

lines: A SICKNESS ON THE TRADE ROUTES.
cards: A sickness moves along the trade routes into Europe. It arrives in a town, and within days families are burying their own. Nobody understands how it spreads.

Doctors argue about bad air and the stars. Priests call for prayer and processions. And in town after town, a rumor arrives as well, sometimes before the sickness itself: the Jews are poisoning the wells.
Today, the Black Death, and what fear did with that rumor.

teach.h: A RUMOR NEEDS SOMEONE TO BLAME.
teach.b: The plague killed rich and poor, Christian and Jew. But the rumor needed someone to blame.
In some places, Jews were arrested and tortured until they confessed to poisoning, and those forced confessions were copied and sent on to other towns as proof. And the killing spread.
In parts of the German lands, in Switzerland, in Alsace, whole communities were murdered, often burned, sometimes before the plague had even reached the town. Some voices pushed back.

Pope Clement the Sixth issued a bull that answered the rumor directly: Jews were dying of the plague like everyone else, and it was raging in places where no Jews lived at all. He ordered that Jews not be harmed.
In town after town, the killing went on anyway.

teach.h: TWO GOATS ON THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.
teach.b: Our line borrows a word from the Day of Atonement, though the Torah means something very different by it. In Leviticus the high priest takes two goats. One is offered.
Over the other he lays his hands and confesses the sins of the people, and the goat is sent off into the wilderness. The Hebrew says it goes to Azazel.
The King James Bible gives the English word: the goat is kept alive "to let him go for a scapegoat into the wilderness." Notice what the ritual does.

The priest names the people's own wrongs, out loud, before the goat goes. At its center is taking responsibility. The plague years ran it backward: a frightened crowd invented guilt and laid it on the people next door.

teach.h: THE PEOPLE NAME THEIR OWN SINS.
teach.b: The goat carried away sins the people had confessed as their own. The Jews of those towns were blamed for sins nobody had committed.

how: On Yom Kippur, Jews read the Torah's account of the two goats in the synagogue service and confess their own wrongs aloud, together, in the first person plural.

games.why: he issued a bull saying exactly that, though in town after town the killing went on.

practice: Think of something going wrong right now, at work, at home or in the news, and notice if your mind has already chosen someone to blame, especially someone who isn't in the room.
Gently set that name down, and ask instead: what part of this is simply hard, and what part is mine?

wordCard.voice: Azazel. Where the Torah's scapegoat is sent in Leviticus, the image behind a plague-year rumor that blamed Jews for the Black Death. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Azazel, where the second goat is sent in Leviticus 16; what the name means is debated.

carryVoice: Your line: no scapegoats. Fear looks for someone to blame; the old rite looked inward. Until tomorrow.
